questions.question: What tokens does tokenize("not great!") return?
options: ["not", "great", "!"]
["not great"]
["not", "great!"]
["not", "great", "positive"]
questions.explanation: TOKEN_RE captures words and the punctuation character ! as separate lowercase tokens.

questions.question: What does apply_negation(["not", "good", "!"]) return?
options: ["NOT_not", "good", "!"]
["not", "NOT_good", "!"]
questions.explanation: The flag turns on at not, prefixes the following content token, and the exclamation mark then resets the flag.

questions.question: What happens to negation after a comma in apply_negation?
options: The comma becomes the new negation word
Negation remains active until the end of the document
The comma is a terminator, so following tokens are no longer prefixed with NOT_
Every token before the comma is deleted
questions.explanation: NEGATION_TERMINATORS includes comma, so the loop sets negate=False when it sees it.

questions.question: Why does train_nb add alpha to every vocabulary count?
options: It forces both class priors to be exactly one half
It removes tokens that appear in only one class
It converts the word probabilities into cosine similarities
Laplace smoothing gives an unseen token a nonzero class-conditional probability
questions.explanation: The numerator counts[w]+alpha and denominator total+alpha*|vocab| prevent zero probabilities for known vocabulary items.

questions.question: How does predict_nb compare a document with the two sentiment classes?
options: It adds the log prior and log probability for each observed token, then chooses the largest score
It counts positive words only and ignores class priors
It averages raw token IDs and thresholds the result at zero
It selects the class whose vocabulary has more unique words
questions.explanation: The function accumulates log(class_priors[cls]) plus log word probabilities and returns the argmax.

questions.question: For y_true=["+","-","+","-"] and y_pred=["+","+","-","-"], what F1 does evaluate report?
questions.explanation: There is one true positive, one false positive, and one false negative; precision and recall are both 0.5, so F1 is 0.5.
